title: Some Underlying Geometric Notions: Simplify, Attach, Extend
notes: Open the deck by naming Chapter 0 as a grammar lesson for the rest of algebraic topology. The course will later compute groups and rings, but first students need reliable geometric moves: simplify a space, attach cells, and extend homotopies without losing control.

title: From Path Homotopy Type To HEP
notes: Use the roadmap as a navigation promise. Simplify means replacing a space by its homotopy type, attach means building with CW skeleta and quotients, and extend means using HEP-style control. The important inspection path starts at path homotopy type and ends at extension technology.

title: Homotopy And Deformation Retraction Are Different Data
notes: Slow down on the word homotopy. A homotopy is a path in a mapping space, so the formula records moving maps rather than a cloud of independent moving points. Deformation retraction is stronger because the motion happens inside one space and fixes the core at the end.

title: Homotopy Equivalence Is Data In Both Directions
notes: This slide separates two-sided and one-sided data. Homotopy equivalence needs maps both ways whose composites are homotopic to identities. A deformation retract supplies a special case, but the retract data includes an inclusion and retraction tied to a chosen subspace.

title: Contractible Need Not Look Instantly Collapsible
notes: The point of this schematic is humility. Tie it to the source's house with two rooms example: contractible does not always mean visually crushable from the picture in front of us. Ask students to identify the target point, then emphasize that the proof is a continuous family of maps from the whole space to itself.

title: The Mapping Cylinder Packages A Map Into Geometry
notes: Present the mapping cylinder as a disciplined replacement for an arbitrary map. We attach a cylinder on X to Y by the top end, and then the vertical fibers slide into Y. This gives the proof technology behind replacing a map by an inclusion followed by a deformation retract.

title: CW Construction: Attach Disks, Track Boundaries
notes: Treat the CW slide as the chapter's finite bookkeeping system. The ladder says spaces are built by dimension, while the characteristic map says each new disk announces where its boundary lands. The checks certify that the boundary signs already behave like a chain complex.

title: Cell Counts Give Euler Characteristic Before Homology
notes: Euler characteristic is introduced here as a trace of cell structure, not yet as a homology theorem. The examples help students see how one cell in every dimension, or only even dimensions, produces different alternating sums before the later algebra arrives.

title: Polygon Quotients: Edge Labels Decide The Surface
notes: Read each polygon as a quotient recipe rather than as a drawing of the final surface. The cell counts are the inspection target: all vertices identified, edge classes counted, one face retained. The three Euler characteristics match the generated chapter checks.

title: Operations Taxonomy: What Gets Kept, What Gets Collapsed?
notes: This taxonomy keeps the operation names from blurring together. Product keeps both coordinates, quotient identifies a prescribed relation, cone and suspension collapse ends, wedge identifies basepoints, and smash combines product with a basepoint collapse. Use it as vocabulary cleanup before the lab.

title: Operation Lab: Cone, Suspension, Wedge
notes: Use the embedded operation lab when teaching live, and use the three fallback targets if the interactive panel is not available. The lesson is to inspect what is unique after quotienting: one cone tip, two suspension points, and a shared wedge basepoint.

title: Collapse A Contractible Subcomplex Without Changing Type
notes: The collapse criterion is where homotopy type becomes a working simplifier. In a CW pair, collapsing a contractible subcomplex behaves well because the inclusion has the right cofibration control. The graph example makes the preserved free rank visible.

title: Attaching Maps And Mapping Cones Record The Same Control Problem
notes: Connect attaching maps to mapping cones as two ways of organizing the same problem: where does the boundary go, and what quotient records the attachment? Homotopic attaching maps give equivalent spaces relative to the old skeleton, which is why attaching data is flexible.

title: Homotopy Extension Property For CW Pairs
notes: HEP is best taught as a rectangle-filling problem. The bottom edge already has a homotopy on X at time zero, and the side strip has a homotopy on A. For CW pairs, those compatible boundary data extend across the full rectangle.

title: Proof Synthesis: The Toolkit Behind Later Invariants
notes: Close by making the proof dependencies explicit. HEP supports controlled collapse, collapse supports attaching-map comparisons, and mapping cylinders package arbitrary maps into better-behaved inclusions. This is the bridge to Chapter 1, where invariants start detecting what survives.
